title: Airbnb Search and Pricing Architecture Review

questions.question: A design exercise assumes 100 million searches per day. Approximately what is the average search rate before applying a peak multiplier?
options: 1,160 searches per second
11,600 searches per second
116,000 searches per second
1 million searches per second
questions.explanation: 100,000,000 divided by 86,400 seconds is about 1,157 searches per second. Capacity planning then applies a separate regional and peak multiplier.

questions.question: Why should geographic retrieval use spatial cells or another geo index before personalized ranking?
options: It finds a broad nearby candidate set without scoring the full listing catalog
It makes inventory revalidation unnecessary
It guarantees the cheapest listing ranks first
It replaces host pricing rules
questions.explanation: Spatial indexing turns a viewport, radius, or destination into a bounded local candidate set. Expensive eligibility and personalization work can then run on hundreds of candidates rather than millions.

questions.question: What is the user-visible trade-off when the availability snapshot TTL is increased?
options: Fewer authority reads and often lower latency, but sold nights can remain in retrieval longer
Higher freshness and higher authority read load
Perfect booking consistency with no revalidation
More personalization with no capacity cost
questions.explanation: A longer-lived projection absorbs more repeated reads, but it expands the maximum stale window. The inventory authority must still reject a sold night before display or booking.

questions.question: A stale price feature causes the ranker to order one listing too highly. Which value may be shown as the current checkout total?
options: Only a non-expired, versioned quote from the pricing authority
The ranker's estimated nightly price
Any cached total from the previous guest
The average price for the geographic cell
questions.explanation: Ranking estimates can influence order, but fees, taxes, discounts, currency, host rules, and quote version belong to the pricing authority. A stale feature may reduce relevance without becoming price truth.

questions.question: What is the safest search fallback when personalization features are unavailable but geography, inventory, and pricing remain healthy?
options: Rank with geographic relevance, listing quality, availability, and market priors
Return no listings to every guest
Skip inventory checks to recover latency
Use another guest's feature vector
questions.explanation: Personalization improves order but is not an authority boundary. A deterministic fallback can preserve valid search results while the system measures degraded relevance and feature-store recovery.

questions.question: Which invariant must still hold when caches, ranking features, or search projections are stale?
options: A bookable result is revalidated by inventory authority and uses a current authoritative price quote
Every listing receives the same rank
The search cache confirms the reservation
The ranking model may create a price when pricing is unavailable
questions.explanation: Search-side data may be eventually consistent to meet latency and scale goals, but it cannot authorize a sold night or fabricate the transaction price. Those decisions remain behind explicit authorities.
